title: Care From a Distance: Indian Families Turn to Eldercare Start-Ups for Ageing Parents
excerpt: As younger Indians move cities and countries for work, a professional eldercare sector — care managers, clinics and community programmes — is taking over work the joint family once did, the BBC reports.
body:
• Changing family structures — adult children working in other cities or abroad — are driving demand in India for start-ups offering medical support and companionship services for ageing parents, the BBC reports.
  • The model that has emerged: a dedicated local care manager who visits, coordinates medical care and reports back to children wherever they live.
  • The scale is long-term: India's elderly population is projected to reach 23 crore by 2036, and the government's Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY) framework reported 764 supported senior citizen homes and a national dashboard listing 30,151 geriatric caregivers.
  • For NRI families: the questions to ask any provider are who shows up in an emergency, how medical escalation works, and how you are informed — before price.

The phone call is familiar to thousands of Indian families: a parent has fallen ill in Pune or Patna, and the children are in Bengaluru, Dubai or New Jersey. The BBC reports that changing family structures in India are now driving a start-up sector built for exactly that call — services offering eldercare, from medical support to companionship, for parents whose children have become mobile.

What the start-ups actually sell

The core product is presence. Providers assign a care manager — a named local person who visits the parent at home, accompanies them to medical appointments, coordinates with doctors and reports back to the family. Around that core sit community and wellbeing programmes and, increasingly, specialist clinical care for healthy ageing. The pitch, made by providers such as Samarth Elder Care — which marked ten years of operation in October — is that most elders want to grow old in their own homes, and the service exists so they do not have to choose between staying home and being safe. Samarth says it operates across more than 350 cities and serves families in over 33 countries, a footprint aimed squarely at the diaspora.

"We started Samarth because we were trying to care for our own parents from a distance," founder Asheesh Gupta said in the company's anniversary statement — a sentence that describes the entire sector's founding condition.

The demographic arithmetic

The market exists because the numbers moved. India's elderly population is projected to reach 23 crore by 2036, and the state is building alongside the start-ups: an official factsheet on the Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY), detailed by Nation Press, counts 764 senior citizen homes, 13 continuous care homes and 17 mobile medicare units supported under the scheme, a SHATAYU dashboard listing 30,151 trained geriatric caregivers, and a SAGE initiative offering equity support of up to Rs 1 crore to selected eldercare start-ups. The Elderline national helpline for senior citizens has operated since October 2021.

What families should check

For an NRI reader evaluating these services for a parent, the useful questions are operational, not promotional. Who is the named care manager, and how often do they physically visit? What happens at 2 a.m. — who takes the hospital call, and how fast are you informed? Are caregivers vetted and trained, and can you see the vetting standard? Does the service cover your parent's city in depth, or through a partner network? And what does the reporting look like — a dashboard and scheduled updates, or silence until something goes wrong? The BBC's reporting describes a sector growing because families need it; the families who get the most from it are the ones who buy the escalation process, not the brochure.
